The strongest continuation is now a positive physical-state construction for an oscillator with both monitored gain and monitored loss. It retains the non-Gaussian information created by the measurements, closes under the actual binary detector instrument, and admits a finite approximation with a bound on the complete feedback record.

The key result is that, for a detector which reports whether any registered event occurred in each bin, the required representation order grows by at most one per clicked bin. Arbitrarily many unobserved gain and loss events can occur between readouts. A separate continuous parameter carries the thermal excitation, and its numerical range grows with integrated gain rather than exponentially with photon occupation.

This extends the pure-gain construction in an important respect: the approximating state is an actual positive density operator. I also found a sharp limitation. Replacing the detector’s “any event” bit by a parity bit can require exponentially larger order in this same representation. The observation rule is therefore part of what selects an effective physical state.

This controls the complete feedback record and any common subsequent quantum test. Both experiments must use the same implemented controller as a function of the exposed history.

The arithmetic is not free. The construction requires certified scalar matrix evaluations, survival differences, binomial probabilities, and parameter subdivisions. Nearly degenerate turning points or tiny probabilities can require additional precision. Positive stochastic rows can be rounded to dyadic probabilities, and their Bayesian weights can be maintained with integer arithmetic; the rounding allowance enters the displayed bound.

A full uniform bit-complexity theorem has not been proved. The proven result is a polynomial state count and quadrature-node bound, with the scalar evaluation and precision tasks identified. It also gives an absolute complete-record guarantee, not uniform conditional accuracy after every arbitrarily rare observation.

7. The resulting state-selection principle and the next obstruction

The strongest justified principle is:

Choose a positive family that is stable under the permitted no-event evolution and registered update maps. Then account for the detector’s internal transitions, and prove both a physical approximation metric and a computable positive update rule.

The oscillator now supplies all of those interfaces in a restricted non-Gaussian regime. It does not merely retain a known control-history function: its finite implementation is a current positive weight vector and controller, updated at each exposed bin.

The distinction exposed by the parity example is consequential. State selection must retain the form of the information created by the instrument. Neither photon occupation, output bit count, Gaussianity, nor polynomial degree alone is enough.

The next substantive obstacle is spatial or multimode coupling. A product of these number-diagonal families already fails under a beam splitter acting on

The next needed lemma is therefore a computable positive joint representation for coupled modes with unequal monitored baths, together with a controlled physical metric. That is a more consequential continuation than refining the one-mode error exponent. The Green-function, critical-spin, fermionic record-law and transient-memory results remain preserved for compatible interfaces; none has been assumed to solve this missing coupling problem.

The present scoped construction is complete at the theorem and certified-example level. Its verification consists of explicit proofs, exact arithmetic, and complementary native-agent audits—not experimental acquisition or external independent review.

The strongest continuation is now a positive physical-state construction for an oscillator with both monitored gain and monitored loss. It retains the non-Gaussian information created by the measurements, closes under the actual binary detector instrument, and admits a finite approximation with a bound on the complete feedback record.

The key result is that, for a detector which reports whether any registered event occurred in each bin, the required representation order grows by at most one per clicked bin. Arbitrarily many unobserved gain and loss events can occur between readouts. A separate continuous parameter carries the thermal excitation, and its numerical range grows with integrated gain rather than exponentially with photon occupation.

This extends the pure-gain construction in an important respect: the approximating state is an actual positive density operator. I also found a sharp limitation. Replacing the detector’s “any event” bit by a parity bit can require exponentially larger order in this same representation. The observation rule is therefore part of what selects an effective physical state.

7. The resulting state-selection principle and the next obstruction

The strongest justified principle is:

Choose a positive family that is stable under the permitted no-event evolution and registered update maps. Then account for the detector’s internal transitions, and prove both a physical approximation metric and a computable positive update rule.

The oscillator now supplies all of those interfaces in a restricted non-Gaussian regime. It does not merely retain a known control-history function: its finite implementation is a current positive weight vector and controller, updated at each exposed bin.

The distinction exposed by the parity example is consequential. State selection must retain the form of the information created by the instrument. Neither photon occupation, output bit count, Gaussianity, nor polynomial degree alone is enough.

The next substantive obstacle is spatial or multimode coupling. A product of these number-diagonal families already fails under a beam splitter acting on ∣1,0⟩|1,0\rangle∣1,0⟩, because the output contains coherence between the two modes. Existing Gaussian-polynomial and stellar representations supply a broader formal family, but their polynomial core and positive mixture can grow rapidly with mode count.

The next needed lemma is therefore a computable positive joint representation for coupled modes with unequal monitored baths, together with a controlled physical metric. That is a more consequential continuation than refining the one-mode error exponent. The Green-function, critical-spin, fermionic record-law and transient-memory results remain preserved for compatible interfaces; none has been assumed to solve this missing coupling problem.

The present scoped construction is complete at the theorem and certified-example level. Its verification consists of explicit proofs, exact arithmetic, and complementary native-agent audits—not experimental acquisition or external independent review.
